plan.interpretation: In 30 minutes of viewing across at most two videos, the learner understands window functions (OVER, PARTITION BY, ranking, frames, LAG/LEAD) well enough to replace their self-join based reports with window function queries in PostgreSQL.
assumptions: Self-join reports are typically things like previous-row comparisons, running totals, and top-N per group, which map to LAG/LEAD, window frames, and ROW_NUMBER/RANK.
Videos should use PostgreSQL or standard SQL syntax that works in PostgreSQL.
Two videos at most means the plan should favor one comprehensive practical video plus optionally one short complementary video, not many small ones.
No practice time is reserved, so the 30 minutes is all watching.

sub_topics.title: OVER() and PARTITION BY: window vs GROUP BY
sub_topics.why: The learner knows GROUP BY aggregates, so the key mental shift is keeping row-level detail while computing aggregates over partitions, which replaces self-joins to aggregated subqueries.

sub_topics.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK for top-N per group
sub_topics.why: Top-N per group and deduplication are common self-join/subquery report patterns that ranking functions replace directly.

sub_topics.title: LAG and LEAD for previous/next row comparisons
sub_topics.why: Comparing a row with its previous or next row is the classic self-join use case, and LAG/LEAD make it a single pass.

sub_topics.title: Running totals and window frames (ORDER BY, ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN)
sub_topics.why: Running totals and moving averages usually require painful self-joins with inequality conditions; frames replace them.

sub_topics.title: Rewriting self-join reports as window function queries
sub_topics.why: The goal is to convert existing reports, so seeing before/after examples of self-join to window function rewrites ties everything together.

This video is about Window Functions in SQL which is also referred to as Analytic Function in some of the RDBMS. SQL Window Functions covered in this video are RANK, DENSE RANK, ROW NUMBER, LEAD, LAG. Also, we see how to use SQL Aggregate functions like MIN, MAX, SUM, COUNT, AVG as window function. 

My Live SQL Bootcamp is back - the first one in over a year! 8 live sessions, Beginner to Advanced, starting Sept 5. Seats are limited 👇 
https://sqlnest.com/bootcamp/Live_SQL_Bootcamp_Beginner_to_Advanced


This video is focused on teaching how to write SQL Queries using different window functions or analytic functions. We go through the syntax of using rank, dense_rank, row_number, lead, lag and max functions as window function.

Over clause is explained in detail in this video. Over clause is used in SQL when we need to use window function. Inside Over clause, we also use Partition By clause and also Order by clause.
Partition By clause is used to specify the column based on which different windows needs to be created.

The window function you learn in this video is applicable to any RDBMS since these functions are commonly used across most of the popular RDBMS such as Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server etc.

pool.title: SQL Running Total, LAG and LEAD, Moving Average, ROWS vs RANGE | Real-Time #6
pool.description:
Real-time SQL interview questions on analytic window functions with complete queries and real output: running totals, the ROWS vs RANGE tie trap, month-over-month change with LAG and LEAD, a 3-month moving average, percent of total with SUM() OVER (), the LAST_VALUE trap, and a monthly growth report.

INTERVIEW QUESTIONS IN THIS VIDEO
1. Finance wants a running total of revenue by order date. How do you calculate it without a self join or a subquery?
2. Your running total of payments shows the same 2,200 on two rows. What is the difference between ROWS and RANGE, and how do you fix the running total?
3. A manager wants month-over-month revenue change. How do you use LAG and LEAD, and what is the trap when a month has no sales?
4. The business wants a 3-month moving average of revenue. How do you write it, and what happens in the first two months?
5. Finance wants each category's percent of total revenue in one query, with no subquery. How do you do it with SUM() OVER ()?
6. You use LAST_VALUE to show the lowest-paid person in each department, but every row just shows itself. Why does LAST_VALUE seem not to work, and what is the fix?
7. Leadership wants one monthly report with revenue, the previous month, the change and the percent growth. How do you write it so a zero month can't break it?

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
• Running total with SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...)
• Running total per customer, and ROWS vs RANGE (the tie trap)
• LAG and LEAD: month-over-month revenue change
• 3-month moving average with a ROWS frame
• Percent of total with SUM(SUM(x)) OVER (), no subquery
• FIRST_VALUE, and fixing LAST_VALUE with UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
• Scenario: monthly growth report with NULLIF

Every answer is a complete query with its real output, and the last one is the monthly growth report a manager will ask you to write on the spot.
[00:24] Question one: how do you calculate a running total of revenue by date? SUM as a window function, with ORDER BY inside the OVER clause. Each row gets its own amount plus every row before it. No self join, and no subquery. The first order is one thousand two hundred and fifty. The second adds three hundred, so the running total is one thousand five hundred and fifty, and so on down the dates.
[00:51] And here's a sanity check you should always do in a real project: the last running total, four thousand seven hundred and fifty, must equal the total revenue for the period. Remember what ORDER BY does inside OVER. It doesn't just sort. It sets a frame, from the first row up to the current row. That frame is the trap in the next question.
[01:54] Question two: how do you calculate a running total per customer, and what's the difference between ROWS and RANGE? Per customer is one more clause: PARTITION BY customer. The running total restarts for every customer. Mei Chen goes six hundred and fifty, nine hundred and twenty five, one thousand one hundred and seventy five.
[02:16] Then Omar starts again from three hundred. Now the trap. When you write ORDER BY without a frame, the default frame is RANGE, from the first row to the current row. And RANGE includes every row with the same ORDER BY value, its peers. Order 1003 was paid in two parts. Ordered by order ID, both payments are peers, so the default frame adds them together: two thousand two hundred twice.
[03:21] The fix: make the ORDER BY unique, and write ROWS explicitly. Now it goes one thousand nine hundred and fifty, then two thousand two hundred. Why both? ROWS alone splits the tie, but in no guaranteed order. Question three: how do you show the month over month change in revenue?
[03:42] First, a CTE with revenue per month. DATE_TRUNC turns every date into the first day of its month. That's Postgres. In SQL Server, use DATE TRUNC, or DATEFROMPARTS on older versions. Then LAG reads the previous row's revenue, and LEAD reads the next row's. The change is simply revenue minus LAG of revenue.
[04:04] February made one thousand eight hundred and fifty. January one thousand five hundred and fifty, so the change is plus three hundred. March dropped by one thousand one hundred and seventy five. January has no previous month, so LAG returns NULL. The pitfall: LAG means the previous row, not the previous month. If a month had no sales, it wouldn't exist in the CTE, and LAG would compare with two months back.
[04:30] In a real report, join to a calendar of months first.
[05:15] Question four: how do you calculate a three month moving average? AVG as a window function, with an explicit frame: ROWS BETWEEN TWO PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. That's this month plus the two before it. March averages January, February and March: one thousand three hundred and fifty eight point three three.
[05:36] April drops January and adds April: nine hundred and fifty. Now look at the first two rows. January averages one month, and February two. I added a COUNT over the same frame to make that visible. If the business wants a true three month average, return NULL until months used is three. Same warning as LAG: ROWS counts rows, not calendar months, so fill the missing months first.
[06:01] In a real project, this is what you put on a dashboard to smooth a noisy trend line.
[06:48] Question five: how do you calculate each category's percent of total revenue, without a subquery? Group revenue by category, as usual. Then SUM of SUM, OVER with empty brackets. The inner SUM is the normal group total. The outer SUM is a window over all the grouped rows, so every row gets the grand total: four thousand seven hundred and fifty.
[07:11] Divide one by the other. Electronics is sixty three point one six percent. Furniture thirty two point six three, and Accessories four point two one. Why does SUM of SUM work? Because window functions run after GROUP BY. That's the logical query order from the first video of this series, and interviewers love to hear you connect the two.
[07:33] Two details: multiply by one hundred point zero, so integer columns don't do integer division. And in a real report, check that the percentages add up to one hundred.
[08:26] Question six: what do FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE do, and why does LAST_VALUE seem not to work? For each employee in Sales and Engineering, we want the top paid and the lowest paid person in the department. FIRST_VALUE, ordered by salary descending, gives the top: Daniel in Sales, Omar in Engineering.
[08:46] Correct on every row. LAST_VALUE with the same window should give the lowest paid. But look at the last default column: every row just returns its own name. That's the default frame again. With ORDER BY, the frame ends at the current row, or its last tie, so here the last value in the frame is the current row itself.
[09:06] The fix: extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, the whole partition. Now every row shows Fatima in Sales and Mei in Engineering. Even simpler, use FIRST_VALUE with the order reversed ascending.
[10:00] And the scenario. Your manager asks: for every month, show the revenue, the previous month's revenue, the change and the percent growth, in one query. Build it in layers, because it's easier to read and to debug. CTE one: revenue per month. CTE two: add the previous month with LAG. Then the final select does the math on plain columns, so LAG is written only once.
[10:25] Percent growth is the change divided by the previous revenue, times one hundred point zero. NULLIF of previous revenue and zero turns a zero into NULL, so a month after a zero month returns NULL, instead of a divide by zero error. February grew nineteen point three five percent. March fell sixty three point five one percent, and June fell eighty three point three three.
[10:49] And two things to tell the manager. January is NULL on purpose: there's no previous month, so growth is unknown, not zero. And if a month ever has no sales, join to a calendar first, so LAG compares the right months.
[11:45] To recap: SUM over ORDER BY gives a running total, and PARTITION BY restarts it per group. The default frame is RANGE: ties add up together. Write ROWS. LAG / LEAD read the previous / next row, not month. Frames drive moving averages and fix LAST_VALUE. SUM(SUM(x)) OVER() = percent of total; NULLIF for growth. In the next video, we answer the questions about duplicates and data cleaning.
[12:08] If this helped, like the video and subscribe to Tech Brothers IT, so you don't miss the rest of this series.

pool.windows:
[00:00] Window functions in SQL allow you to perform complex calculations across related rows while preserving the granular detail of your original data set, unlike traditional aggregate methods. When you need to keep individual records visible while also calculating aggregate metrics like totals or averages, window functions provide the ideal solution.
[00:20] Standard group by clauses collapse your data into single summary rows. Window functions solve this compromise by attaching calculations to every original row instead. Think of a window function as an analytical process that works in the background, attaching new insights to each row without merging or losing your specific transaction records. The core syntax requires a function followed by the over clause.
[00:43] You can then use partition by to isolate windows and order by to define processing sequences. An empty over clause instructs SQL to treat your entire table as one giant window, appending a grand total to every row in your result set. By applying an empty over clause to a sum calculation, you can easily compare individual transaction amounts against the grand total of all company sales.
[01:43] The real power comes from partition by, which divides data into distinct, isolated windows. Calculations then reset automatically for each specific regional group. With partitioning, the total sales calculation adapts to each region's boundaries, providing context-aware metrics while maintaining visibility into every individual sale. Remember, use group by when you need to summarize high-level data, but reach for window functions when your goal is to analyze data while keeping the full detail.
[02:10] Adding an order by clause inside the over function allows you to process rows sequentially, which is essential for rolling history, moving averages, and cumulative sums. Using sum with an order by clause creates a dynamic running total that accumulates transaction values as it moves chronologically through your data. The RO_NUMBER function assigns a unique, sequential integer to each row.
[02:32] Even in the case of a tie, it ensures every row gets a distinct identifier. If you need to acknowledge ties logically, use rank instead.
[03:19] It assigns the same rank to identical values, though it will leave gaps in your sequential numbering. For a sequence without gaps, DENSE_RANK is your go-to. It gives tied rows the same rank while ensuring the next rank immediately follows, regardless of ties. Understanding how RO_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK behave is crucial.
[03:39] While all three rank data, they differ significantly in how they handle ties and whether they leave gaps in the numbering sequence. You can combine partition by and order by within an over clause to perform localized rankings. This effectively resets the rank for each group, letting you identify top performers within specific regions. This pattern is a highly efficient way to solve top-end problems.
[04:00] By ranking items within their respective groups, you avoid the overhead of complex joins while quickly isolating your top performers. Positional functions like LAG allow you to look at data from previous rows. It is an essential tool for tracking period-over-period changes and trends without needing manual data alignment. Going a step further, you can combine LAG with subtraction to calculate variances directly in your query.
[04:22] This makes tracking growth and shifts over time a clean and simple process. For forward-looking analysis, use the LEAD function. Just as LAG looks back, LEAD pulls data from future rows, which is perfect for predictive modeling or planning your next operational steps. Window functions are versatile enough to integrate with conditional logic. By pairing a ranking function with a case statement, you can dynamically categorize your data based on relative performance metrics.
[04:47] Remember that SQL follows a specific order of execution. You cannot directly filter on window functions in a WHERE clause because they are processed after raw data has already been filtered. Beyond simple ranking, these functions are the engine behind modern analytics. From smoothing trends with moving averages to defining active user sessions, they bring complex intelligence to your daily reporting.
[05:08] When building these queries, avoid common pitfalls like confusing partitioning with grouping, forgetting to order your data, or trying to filter by window results before they are computed. Let's test your knowledge. Which of these ranking functions keeps ranks identical for tied values but ensures there are no gaps in the final sequence? That is the hallmark of DENSE_RANK.
[05:28] Time to practice. Use the sales dataset to apply these ranking and positional functions, calculating cumulative totals, identifying top performers, and measuring variants across your regional data. Keep this cheat sheet handy. It covers the core syntax and the critical model that explains why window functions are superior for preserving detail while summarizing your metrics.
[05:49] Congratulations on finishing Day 15. You have mastered powerful analytical tools and are ready to tackle complex SQL challenges in our next session on common table expressions.

In this video, we solve 15 real SQL interview questions (SET 2) using a single shared dataset - Employees, Departments, Users, Categories, Products, Orders, and SalaryHistory. You'll see how to sort records with ORDER BY, limit results with TOP/LIMIT, safely wipe a table with TRUNCATE, enforce uniqueness with PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints, prevent NULL values, combine tables with UNION, find the second highest salary using DENSE_RANK, list departments with zero employees using LEFT JOIN, find the top-selling category with GROUP BY, match employees to managers with a self-join, filter aggregates with HAVING, build a dynamic PIVOT when category names aren't known in advance, calculate year-over-year salary growth with LAG, and generate a consecutive date series using a Recursive CTE — no calendar table required. Every query is written and explained against real table structures with real inserted data, so you can copy, run, and understand exactly why each solution works.

✅ Sorting and limiting rows the right way (ORDER BY, TOP, LIMIT) 
✅ TRUNCATE vs DELETE — when to use which 
✅ PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE constraints explained with examples 
✅ Enforcing NOT NULL and unique usernames at the database level ✅ UNION vs UNION ALL and when duplicates actually matter 
✅ Finding the Nth highest salary using DENSE_RANK 
✅ LEFT JOIN trick to find "missing" records (departments with no employees) 
✅ Self-joins to compare employees with their managers 
✅ WHERE vs HAVING — the #1 aggregate filter mistake 
✅ Dynamic PIVOT for unknown/changing category names

pool.title: How to Use Window Functions for High-Performance Postgres Queries
pool.description:
Are you still relying on slow self-joins or complex subqueries to perform analytical tasks in PostgreSQL? It’s time to upgrade your SQL game. In this video, we dive into PostgreSQL Window Functions—the secret weapon for writing cleaner, faster, and more efficient queries.

Whether you are performing rolling averages, calculating running totals, or ranking data, window functions allow you to perform calculations across a set of table rows that are related to the current row, without collapsing them into a single output row. We’ll show you how to identify bottlenecks in your current SQL and replace them with high-performance windowed operations.

In this video, you will learn:

The difference between GROUP BY and window functions.

How to use essential window functions like ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), LEAD(), and LAG().

Real-world performance tuning: Replacing inefficient joins with window functions.

Best practices for writing readable and performant analytical SQL

[00:00] (chapter) The GROUP BY Dilemma: Why SQL Needed Window Functions
[01:05] (chapter) Deconstructing the OVER() Clause: PARTITION BY vs ORDER BY
[02:18] (chapter) The Ranking Trio: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK

[05:05] (chapter) Time-Travel Analytics: LEAD and LAG Functions

[07:35] (chapter) Database Engine Internals: B-Tree Index Optimization for WindowAgg
[00:00] In relational database engineering, the traditional group by clause has one major drawback. It collapses all individual rows into summary buckets. If your company has 1,000 employees across 10 departments, running a group by department returns exactly 10 rows. This makes it impossible to see an individual engineer's salary side by side with their department's average or calculate how their earnings rank against their peers, without resorting to slow, expensive self-joins.
[00:28] SQL window functions solve this fundamental problem. A window function performs calculations across a specified set of table rows, known as a window frame, while preserving the unique identity of every single underlying row. In this master class, you will learn the exact mechanics of the over clause, ranking algorithms, and time travel analytics.
[00:49] Every window function relies on the over clause. The over clause defines the boundaries of the calculation window using two primary keywords, partition by and order by.
[01:40] Partition by divides your data set into logical groups, exactly like a group by, but without collapsing rows. If you partition by department, the database isolates each department into its own computation partition. Order by defines the evaluation sequence of rows inside each partition. When order by is present inside the over clause, it changes aggregate functions like sum and AVG into cumulative running totals.
[02:07] Under the hood, the database engine maintains an active calculation frame, sliding from the first row of the partition down to the current row being processed. In FNG technical interviews, interviewers frequently ask candidates to explain the difference between row_number, rank, and dense_rank. The distinction comes down to how each function handles identical tie values.
[02:29] Row_number assigns a strictly unique, sequential integer to every row, starting from one. Even if two engineers earn the exact same salary, row_number arbitrarily assigns one as rank one and the other as rank two.
[03:24] Rank assigns the same number to tied values, but skips subsequent rank numbers to maintain position integrity. If two rows tie for first place, they both receive rank one and the next row jumps to rank three. Dense_rank assigns the same number to ties without skipping numbers. The tied rows both receive rank one, and the very next row receives rank two.
[03:47] Whenever an interviewer asks for the top n values, dense_rank is usually the required production choice. A standard enterprise question is, find the top two highest paid employees in each department. Junior engineers often attempt to write where row_number over equals two. This query instantly crashes with a syntax error.
[04:09] Why? Because in SQL query execution order, the where clause is evaluated in step three, while window functions are not evaluated until step six, after where, group by, and having have finished.
[05:02] To filter on a window function, you must wrap the calculation inside a common table expression, or CTE, or an inline subquery. You compute the rank inside the CTE, and then apply your where rank equals two filter in the outer query. This two-tier pattern is the universal production standard. In financial analytics and time series reporting, you frequently need to compare the current row's value with a previous or upcoming row.
[05:29] Historically, developers solved this with painful self-joins on timestamps. SQL provides two specialized navigation functions, LAG and LEAD. LAG peers backwards, accessing data from previous rows without a self-join. You can fetch last month's revenue to calculate month-over-month growth percentage in a single pass.
[05:50] LEAD peers forwards, looking into upcoming rows. This is ideal for tracking user session funnels, measuring how long a customer remained on a page before clicking the next event.
[06:41] Both functions take an optional offset number and a fallback default value to handle null boundaries. Window aggregates unlock sophisticated financial accounting queries with minimal code. By pairing sum with an order by clause, you generate running totals such as account balances and year-to-date sales. You can also fine-tune your window frame using the rows between specification.
[07:05] For instance, specifying rows between six preceding and current row transforms an AVG calculation into a seven-day rolling moving average, smoothing out weekend volatility in web traffic metrics. These operations run entirely in memory across the partition, making them orders of magnitude faster than iterative application-level loops.
[07:25] How does a database engine like PostgreSQL or MySQL execute window functions under the hood? In an explain execution plan, you will observe a window ag operator. If your table lacks appropriate indexes, the database must perform an expensive disk sort to group the partition columns and sort the order columns, causing CPU and disk IO bottlenecks.
[08:27] To make your window functions lightning fast, create a composite B-tree index where the leading columns match the partition by expression, followed immediately by the order by columns. This allows the database to stream pre-sorted index pages directly into the window ag node with zero disk sorting. Mastering window functions elevates you from writing basic SQL to architecting high-performance enterprise analytics.

 - Classify employees into performance categories (High, Solid, Emerging, etc.)

We calculate team-wide averages and compare each employee’s performance based on:
 - Number of sales
 - Total items sold
 - Total revenue generated
 - Then we rank employees and label them as:
          High Performer
          Solid Performer
          Competent Performer
          Emerging Performer

This is the kind of SQL logic you’ll see in real data analyst and data engineer jobs.

Beginners learning SQL from scratch

pool.title: SQL Window Functions Explained: OVER, PARTITION BY, RANK, LAG, Running Totals
pool.description:
SQL window functions explained with real examples: the OVER clause, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY inside OVER, ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK, running totals with SUM OVER, LAG and LEAD for month over month change, and moving averages with ROWS BETWEEN. We rank sales reps per region without losing a single row, and check every answer by hand. All data in this video is made up for teaching, not real company data.

If this video helped you, please like, share and subscribe to CodeFlow Daily.

Key ideas:
GROUP BY folds rows; a window function keeps every row and adds a column
SUM(amount) OVER () = grand total on every row
SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) = total per region
ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3,4 | RANK 1,2,2,4 | DENSE_RANK 1,2,2,3
SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) = running total
revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) = month over month change
AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) = 3 month moving average

[00:00] Here is a question that sounds simple. You have a sales table and for every region you want to rank the sales reps from best to worst. But you also want to keep every single row so you can still see each rep's name and amount right next to their rank.
[00:20] If you reach for group by, you lose the rows. Each region collapses into a single line. This is exactly the job window functions were made for. A window function looks at a group of related rows, does a calculation across them and then writes the answer back onto every row without collapsing anything.
[00:46] In this video we will use a small made-up sales table, so every number is easy to check by hand. We will compare group by with window functions, then learn the over clause, partition by, and order by inside over.
[01:43] Then row number, rank and dense rank, running totals, lag and lead, and finally moving averages. Let's begin. Let's start with the difference because it is the key idea. Here is our made-up table. Six rows, two regions, North and South with a rep name and a sale amount for each row.
[02:09] If we write select region, sum of amount from sales group by region, SQL squeezes each region down to one row. North becomes 1300 and South becomes 1100. That is useful but look at what we lost.
[02:29] The rep names are gone. You cannot see who sold what anymore. Now look at the window version. Select region, rep, amount, and sum of amount over partition by region.
[03:24] This time we still get all six rows. Each row keeps its own name and its own amount, and the region total simply appears in a new column beside it. Every North row shows 1300 and every South row shows 1100. So remember it this way.
[03:46] Group by folds rows together. A window function keeps the rows and adds a column. The part that turns a normal function into a window function is the word over. You write the function like sum of amount, then over, then a pair of brackets.
[04:06] The brackets describe the window, which is the set of rows the function is allowed to look at. The simplest case is empty brackets. Sum of amount over with nothing inside means the window is the whole result.
[05:03] Every row looks at all six rows, add them up and gets 2400. So each row now shows the grand total right beside its own amount. That alone is handy. For example, you can divide amount by that total to get each rep's share of all sales.
[05:25] Asha sold 500 out of 2400, which is about 21%. Inside the brackets you can add three things. Partition by, which splits the rows into groups. Order by, which sorts the rows inside each group. And a frame which picks a slice of rows around the current one.
[05:50] We will take them one at a time. First, Partition by. Partition by region tells SQL to cut the table into separate windows, one per region.
[06:43] Think of it as drawing a fence around the North rows and another fence around the South rows. The function then runs inside each fence on its own and it never looks over the fence. So for the first North row, the window is just the four North rows.
[07:04] 500, 300, 300 and 200 add up to 1300. For a South row, the window is just the two South rows, 700 and 400, which makes 1100. Notice that Partition by looks a lot like Group by. Both split rows into groups using the same column.
[07:28] The difference is what happens after that. Group by returns one row per group. Partition by keeps every row and only changes what each row can see.
[08:22] You can also partition by more than one column, for example, region and year to get smaller windows. Next, Order by inside over. This sorts the rows inside each window and it is completely separate from the order by at the end of your query.
[08:42] The one inside over decides the order the function walks through the rows. The one at the end only decides how the final result is displayed. Order matters a lot for some functions. Ranking needs it because rank one only makes sense once you know what best means.
[09:04] Here we sort the North rows by amount, highest first. Asha with 500 comes first, then Ravi and Meera with 300, then Dave with 200. There is one surprise you should know about.
[10:01] When you add order by to sum over, the sum stops being a total and becomes a running sum. That is because the default window now runs from the first row up to the current row, and rows that tie on the sort value are counted together. Here Ravi and Meera tie, so both show 1100.
[10:24] We will use running sums on purpose soon, but if you only wanted a total, leave order by out. Now the most popular window functions, the ranking ones. All three need order by inside over. We partition by region and order by amount, highest first.
[10:45] Row number simply counts the rows. One, two, three, four. It never repeats even when two amounts are the same. Ravi and Meera both sold 300, but row number still gives them two and three, and which one gets two is not guaranteed.
[11:46] Rank treats ties fairly. Ravi and Meera both get rank two. Then rank skips a number, so Dave gets rank four, the way a race skips a place after a tie. Dense rank also gives both of them two, but it does not skip, so Dave gets rank three.
[12:07] And in South, John is first and Priya is second because each region ranks on its own. So which one should you pick? Use row number when you need exactly one row per position, like the top seller in each region. Use rank or dense rank when ties should share a place.
[12:32] Let's switch to a second made-up table. Monthly revenue for one shop from January to June.
[13:20] 100, 120, 90, 150, 130 and 170. A running total answers a simple question. How much have we earned so far? We write sum of revenue over order by month.
[13:40] For January, the window is just January, so the total is 100. For February, the window grows to cover January and February, giving 220. March adds 90, giving 310. April brings it to 460.
[14:00] May makes it 590. And June ends at 760, which is the full half year. See how the window starts at the top and stretches down one row at a time. If you had many shops, you would add partition by shop, and each shop would get its own running total that restarts from zero.
[15:05] Running totals are perfect for year to date numbers and for tracking progress toward a target. Often you want to compare a row with its neighbor. Did revenue go up or down since last month? That is what lag and lead do. Lag of revenue over order by month reaches back one row and fetches the previous value.
[15:31] For February, lag returns the January value 100. For March, it returns the February value 120. January has no row before it, so lag gives null there. Now subtract. Revenue minus lag of revenue gives the change.
[15:53] February is up 20, March is down 30, April is up 60, May is down 20, and June is up 40.
[16:43] Lead is the mirror image. It looks forward one row instead of back, so the last row, June, gets null. Both functions take two optional extras. A distance, like lag of revenue, comma two to look back two rows. And a default value, like zero to use instead of null.
[17:07] This is the cleanest way to get month over month change without writing a self join. Last tool, the moving average. Monthly numbers jump around and a moving average smooths them out. Here we want a three-month average. We write average of revenue over order by month, rows between two preceding and current row.
[17:34] That frame clause is the key. It says for each row, take the current row plus the two rows before it.
[18:23] For March, the window is January, February and March. 100 + 120 + 90 is 310, divided by three, about 103. Then the window slides down. For April, it covers February, March and April, and the average is 120.
[18:47] For May, it is about 123. For June, it is 150. Notice the first two months have fewer than three rows, so their averages use only what exists. Plot it and the line is much smoother than the bars.
[19:08] Rows between counts physical rows. There is also range between, which works on values instead, but rows is easier to reason about, so start there.
[20:00] Let's wrap up. A window function calculates across related rows and keeps every row. Group by folds rows, a window adds a column. The over clause defines the window. Partition by splits it into groups. Order by sorts the rows inside each group.
[20:23] Row number, rank and dense rank handle positions and ties. Sum over order by gives you running totals. Lag and lead compare a row with its neighbors. And rows between gives you sliding windows, like moving averages.
[20:43] To practice, make a tiny table of your own, try each function on it, and check every answer by hand just like we did today. If this video helped you, please like, share and subscribe to Code Flow Daily. See you in the next one.

SQL Window Functions covered in this video are FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE, NTILE, CUME_DIST and PERCENT_RANK. Also we cover how to use FRAME Clause while writing SQL Queries using window function. We also look at alternate way of writing SQL Query using window function. 

We discuss in detail about the Frame clause and how RANGE is different from ROWS and how to use Unbounded Preceding and Unbounded Following while using certain window functions.

This is the second video where we talk about window functions in SQL. I have made another video covering other window functions such as RANK, DENSE RANK, LEAD, LAG and ROW NUMBER. Link to the previous video is mentioned below:

We look at how to use WINDOW clause while writing SQL query using window functions. We talk about the OVER clause and how partition by clause can impact the result set.

Partition By clause is used to specify the column based on which different windows needs to be created.
